content: Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN) is a condition characterized by rapid breathing and signs of respiratory distress. It typically manifests within the first two hours of life in term and late preterm infants. Although TTN is generally self-limiting, it has been associated with an increased risk of wheezing syndromes later in childhood. The use of salbutamol (albuterol) for TTN is based on evidence suggesting that β-agonists can enhance the clearance of alveolar fluid, potentially improving respiratory function. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of salbutamol compared to placebo, no treatment, or other drugs in infants born at 34 weeks’ gestational age or later who were diagnosed with TTN. The primary outcomes assessed included the duration of oxygen therapy, the need for continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), and the need for mechanical ventilation. The review also considered the duration of hospital stay and respiratory support as secondary outcomes. The search strategy included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, covering studies published up to April 2020. Abstracts from major perinatal and pediatric congresses and clinical trial registries were also reviewed. Randomized controlled trials, quasi-randomized controlled trials, and cluster trials were included if they compared salbutamol with placebo, no treatment, or other drugs in infants less than three days old with TTN. Seven trials involving 498 infants met the inclusion criteria. All studies compared nebulized salbutamol with normal saline. Four studies administered a single dose of salbutamol, while two studies provided three to four doses, and one study allowed additional doses as needed. The certainty of the evidence was rated as low for the duration of hospital stay and very low for other outcomes. Among the primary outcomes, four trials (338 infants) reported the duration of oxygen therapy, with a mean reduction of 19.24 hours (95% confidence interval [CI]: -23.76 to -14.72) in the salbutamol group. One trial (46 infants) assessed the need for CPAP, showing a risk ratio (RR) of 0.73 (95% CI: 0.38 to 1.39) and a risk difference (RD) of -0.15 (95% CI: -0.45 to 0.16). Three trials (254 infants) evaluated the need for mechanical ventilation, with an RR of 0.60 (95% CI: 0.13 to 2.86) and an RD of -0.01 (95% CI: -0.05 to 0.03). The duration of hospital stay (four trials, 338 infants) and respiratory support (two trials, 228 infants) were shorter in the salbutamol group, with mean differences of -1.48 days (95% CI: -1.8 to -1.16) and -9.24 hours (95% CI: -14.24 to -4.23), respectively. One trial (80 infants) reported on the duration of mechanical ventilation and pneumothorax, but the data could not be extracted due to unclear reporting. The authors concluded that the evidence regarding the benefits and harms of salbutamol for TTN is limited and of low certainty. It remains unclear whether salbutamol reduces the duration of oxygen therapy, tachypnea, or the need for CPAP and mechanical ventilation. Salbutamol may slightly reduce the length of hospital stay, but the overall safety and efficacy of this treatment for TTN could not be determined. Five additional trials are ongoing, which may provide further insights into this topic.
